_STATUS_2026_07_28: THE ARM MOVED AND IS NOW CLAMPED DOWN. Kyle relocated it from the return to the MAIN TABLE and fixed it in place, which satisfies 716.4's first invariant: everything expressed in base coordinates is only valid while the base cannot shift. The arm position below is MEASURED and is the new datum to build the cell around. THE CAMERAS ARE NOT: both were nulled out on this date because they were positioned for the old layout on the return and the arm is now on a different table, so every previously-measured camera number describes a geometry that no longer exists. arm._comment: Arm base centre, MEASURED 2026-07-28 by Kyle, clamped down. His words: 'on the main table, front edge, centered at 19.75 inches from the extent edge, the m1 center is 2.25in inset from the edge, arm is clamped down'. DERIVATION into this datum, written out because both axes had a plausible wrong reading. x CORRECTED 2026-07-28: the tape reading of 2.25 in put the back of the base 0.499 in PAST the table edge in the model, and Kyle confirmed 'yes its flush, assume my measurement was off a little so shift accordingly'. So x is now fixed by the FLUSH CONSTRAINT rather than by the tape: the base rear sits 69.82 mm (2.7487 in) behind the m1 axis (measured off the mesh), so a flush rear at the 27.5 in edge puts m1 at 27.5 - 2.7487 = 24.7513. That is a stiffer constraint than a tape to a rounded feature - the arm is physically registered against the edge, and the number now follows the geometry that made it flush. The original reading is kept here because it is the reason the error was findable at all. y = 82 - 19.75 = 62.25, measured from the table's FREE far end. The other reading of 'the extent edge' - 19.75 from y=0 - is ruled out twice over: y=0 is the SIDE WALL, not an edge you can put a tape on, and at y=19.75 the return surface is contiguous at x=27.5, so there would be no 'front edge' to inset 2.25 from. Both of Kyle's phrases only parse together at y=62.25.
arm._yaw_two_numbers: TWO ANGLES, and confusing them put the arm 9.3 deg askew in the viewer until Kyle spotted it on 2026-07-28: 'the back edged of the base is parallel with the table edge, you have it off angle a few degrees'. `base_square_to_deg` is the MEASURABLE one - the bench direction the base is squared to, which is what a person actually sets when clamping it down. 180 = the back edge parallel to the table's front edge, arm facing the back wall. `yaw_deg` is what the code consumes, and by an old and deliberate convention it means the direction the arm REACHES at pan zero, which is NOT the same thing: this model reaches 9.2983 deg off its own base axis (Twin.reach_yaw_deg, measured from the mesh, because the SO-100 and SO-101 disagree by 90). So yaw_deg = 180 + 9.2983 = 189.2983. DERIVED, not measured - if the arm model is ever swapped, reach_yaw changes and this number is stale, which is why _selftest_arm_base_square asserts the built model's base really is square to base_square_to_deg and fails loudly if it drifts.
arm._xy_is_the_m1_axis: x/y locate the M1 AXIS (the shoulder_pan pivot), because that is the one feature on a real arm you can put a tape to and it is what Kyle measured. It is NOT the model's root body origin, which sits 38.8 mm away - attaching the model at these coordinates directly put the real pivot 1.5 in from where it was measured, which Kyle saw as 'a little bit in'. bench_scene now back-solves the attach origin from this axis via Twin.m1_offset_m. Base-relative checks cannot catch that class of error because they move with the arm.
arm._m1_height_reconciled: RESOLVED 2026-07-28, and the 'discrepancy' was mine, not Kyle's. He measured the centre of the m1 MOTOR at 2 in above the table top. I compared that against 62.4 mm and called it an 11.6 mm disagreement. 62.4 mm is the shoulder_pan JOINT ORIGIN - the point the kinematics rotate about - and this repo says 'm1 centre' when it means that joint origin, which is 18 mm away from the centre of the servo body. Kyle asked the right question: 'are you sure what you are checking against is the center?' It was not. Computed off the mesh at qpos 0, measured from the LOWEST base geometry (what a tape resting on the table actually reads): m1 servo body centre 46.5 mm = 1.83 in; joint origin 64.8 mm = 2.55 in. Against his 2.00 in the real gap is 4.3 mm, which is what reading a tape to the nearest inch on a 40 mm-tall motor looks like. The model and the bench agree; nothing was changed. SEPARATE ISSUE the check did expose: the base mesh's lowest point is 2.4 mm BELOW world z=0 while simcam asserts z=0 is the table, so the twin has the arm sunk 2.4 mm into the tabletop. Real, small, and left alone deliberately - see 716.4.

cameras.name: bench
cameras.notes: PLANNED, NOT MEASURED - drawn in amber so the intent can be looked at before anything is drilled (Kyle 2026-07-28: 'add the camera locations to the mujoco so I can see them and the LoS you intend'). Uses the ALREADY PRINTED 60 deg wall bracket on the back wall, on the arm's own line (along 62.25 = the arm's y), lens 26.6 in above the top. That height puts the optical axis on the work-zone centre; 45 deg at 15.3 in is the alternative and trades 30 deg off nadir for 45 but gains resolution (2.33 vs 1.65 px/mm). standoff 2.0 is still a PLACEHOLDER, not a measurement - it shifts the sight line without changing its angle. WHY THE BACK WALL: the arm reaches toward it, so targets are always between the camera and the arm, and the arm cannot occlude them at the moment of grasp - the failure a true overhead view has. Clears the shelf (underside 36.5) by ~10 in, and sits 578 mm from m1 against a 376 mm reach, so the arm cannot strike it. POSITION RETIRED 2026-07-28, not lost - see _STATUS_2026_07_28. It was on the SIDE wall at along 51.5, lens centre z 29.0 above the top, tilted 60 deg down, standoff never measured; the z was genuinely measured on 2026-07-26. Those numbers are kept here as history and must not be reinstated: they placed the camera relative to an arm that stood on the RETURN, and the arm is now on the main table roughly 42 in away, so the old pose points at empty bench. Nulled rather than adjusted because there is no arithmetic that turns a measurement of the old layout into a measurement of the new one. Re-measure after mounting; targets are in 713.9 (overhead: ~504 mm above the table, near-nadir, centred on the work zone - which is LOWER than the 29 in it was at). Registry entry for the live camera is cameras.json - this is only where it is in space.

cameras.name: side
cameras.notes: PLANNED, NOT MEASURED - amber in the viewer. FREE-STANDING rather than on a wall: it is the table-edge stand of 717.5, clamped flush to the outboard edge at x=27.5 with the lens 2.953 in (75 mm) above the top. y=44.0 is set by REACH, not by optics: at 16 in along the edge the arm passes within 36 mm of the camera and at 12-14 in it can strike it outright, so 18.25 in buys 93 mm of clearance for a little resolution (2.43 px/mm, 40 mm tag ~97 px). yaw 119.1 aims it at the work-zone centre; the angle is steep because a camera ON the edge can only see the work zone diagonally, and squaring it to the edge in line with the arm would stare straight down the reach axis with the arm in the way. -y side chosen because +y leaves only 1.5 in of table beyond it. Re-aim once 716.4 places the nest and bins - the stand's tilt and yaw are generator parameters, not literals. SECOND CAMERA, added 2026-07-27. Position has never been measured and stays NULL - the sim will not draw it, which is correct behaviour rather than a gap: an invented pose renders a sight line that looks like evidence. NAME AND ROLE ARE STILL PROVISIONAL, taken from what its first frame showed rather than from Kyle. It has NO MOUNT AT ALL (717.5) and is currently offline. Target from 713.9: ~90 deg azimuth from the arm's reach axis, ~268 mm standoff, 100-200 mm above the table - never on the base side looking down the reach axis, where the arm blocks everything it reaches for. Worth keeping a low angle wherever it lands: the overhead camera cannot resolve HEIGHT above the table and this one can, which is what a grasp approach needs, and it is the only fixed viewpoint that still sees the target when the arm reaches over it.
